title: Chatbots Have Failed People in Crisis — and Nobody Can Audit Why
hook: Clinicians say AI companies are sitting on the data that would show how their chatbots handle users in crisis. Without it, nobody outside the company can tell whether the safeguards work.
key_points: Ars Technica reports clinicians and researchers want AI firms to open up their safety data.
There are documented cases of chatbots responding badly to people in crisis.
Safety claims are currently unverifiable from outside the companies that make the models.
Crisis handling is hard: a model must recognize risk, then refuse to improvise.
Practical rule for you: a chatbot is not a crisis line — use a human hotline.
content_html: There are now documented cases of AI chatbots responding badly to people in acute distress, and Ars Technica reports that clinicians and researchers are pressing AI companies to release the safety data that would show how often it happens and whether new safeguards actually help. Right now, the companies are the only ones who can see it.
extra_html: Two things are worth separating here. The first is a measurement problem: when a company says "we improved crisis handling," there is no independent way to check, because the transcripts, the incident counts, and the internal evaluations stay in-house. Researchers who study self-harm and suicide prevention are used to auditable data, and they don't have it for the tool millions of people now talk to at 2 a.m. The second is a design problem. A language model's whole instinct is to keep producing a fluent, cooperative reply — and in a crisis the correct behavior is close to the opposite: recognize the risk, stop improvising, and route the person to a human. Bolting that reflex onto a system built to always have something to say is genuinely difficult, which is why the practical advice hasn't changed. A chatbot can be a place to put words at an hour when nobody else is awake. It is not a crisis line, and if things are serious, the number to call is a human one.

related.title: AI & Mental Health
related.hook: A chatbot that listens at 2 a.m. without judgment is a real comfort to many. It's also not a therapist, not a crisis line, and not your friend — and confusing the two can be dangerous.

related.title: AI Companions & Friends
related.hook: Millions now have an AI friend, partner, or confidant that's always available and always on their side. It can ease loneliness — and quietly reshape what we expect from real people.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

prereqs.title: AI & Mental Health
prereqs.hook: A chatbot that listens at 2 a.m. without judgment is a real comfort to many. It's also not a therapist, not a crisis line, and not your friend — and confusing the two can be dangerous.

flashcards.prompt: Why do researchers want access to AI companies' safety data?
flashcards.back_html: Because without it, a company's claim that its chatbot handles crisis conversations safely can't be checked by anyone outside the company.

flashcards.prompt: What's the safest way to treat a chatbot when someone is in real distress?

choices.text: As a stopgap for talking, never as a substitute for a crisis line or clinician
As a therapist, since it's available at any hour
As a diagnostic tool that can assess how serious the risk is

flashcards.explanation_html: Chatbots can be a comfort to talk to, but they aren't accountable, trained, or able to escalate. Crisis situations need a human on the other end.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a crisis conversation especially hard for a language model?

choices.text: It must recognize danger and then stop generating plausible-sounding advice
Crisis language uses words the model has never seen
Models are forbidden by law from discussing emotions

flashcards.explanation_html: A model's default behavior is to produce a fluent, agreeable continuation — exactly the wrong instinct when the right move is to stop and hand off to a human.
